subject: Chemistry
title: Poison Dart Frog: Batrachotoxin
description: A micro-lesson that makes Poison Dart Frog: Batrachotoxin usable.

hook.text: The golden poison frog has enough toxin on its skin to kill 10 grown adults. Don't touch.

buildup.text: The toxin is batrachotoxin. The frogs don't make it—they get it from eating toxic beetles.

discovery.text: Batrachotoxin forces sodium channels to stay open. Nerves fire uncontrollably and the heart goes into fibrillation.

twist.text: Captive-bred poison frogs are harmless because they never eat the toxic beetles. The poison is dietary.

climax.text: Indigenous Chocó people rub dart tips on the frog's back. The coating stays lethal for over two years.

punchline.text: A dietary toxin. No beetles, no poison. The frog is just a carrier.

quiz.question: Where does the poison dart frog get its toxin?
options: From eating toxic beetles—captive frogs without the diet are harmless
It produces the toxin in special skin glands
It absorbs it from toxic plants in the rainforest

details.summary: Batrachotoxin from poison dart frogs irreversibly opens voltage-gated sodium channels in nerves and muscles, causing sustained depolarization that leads to heart failure. A single golden poison frog carries enough toxin to kill ten adult humans through skin contact alone.
details.whyItMatters: Indigenous Colombians use batrachotoxin on blowdart tips for hunting. The toxin's mechanism has advanced scientific understanding of sodium channel function and potential therapeutic applications.
takeaways: Batrachotoxin locks sodium channels permanently open in nerve cells
One golden poison frog contains enough poison to kill ten people
The frogs acquire toxin from their diet of specific toxic insects

faq.question: Why are captive-bred poison dart frogs not toxic?
faq.answer: Poison dart frogs do not produce batrachotoxin themselves. They bioaccumulate it from their diet of specific toxic beetles and ants found only in their natural habitat. Captive frogs fed on fruit flies and crickets never develop toxicity.

faq.question: How do indigenous hunters use batrachotoxin without poisoning themselves?
faq.answer: Hunters hold frogs with leaves and apply the skin secretions to dart tips without direct skin contact. The toxin must enter the bloodstream through a wound to be lethal. Meat from animals killed by blowdarts is safe to eat because the small toxin amount degrades with cooking.
